Chapter 3: The Impact of Societal and Cultural Pressures
Burnout doesn’t just happen out of nowhere. The world we live in—our homes, our workplaces, our communities—all shape the way we experience stress, and how easily we can recover from it.
But if you’re a woman, there’s often an extra layer to all of this. Society and culture pile on expectations that make escaping stress even tougher.
Think about it. From the time they’re young, girls are often taught to be what some call “human givers.” They’re encouraged to put everyone else first, to always be agreeable, and to set their own desires aside.
This message shows up everywhere—on TV, in families, at work, and even in advice from friends who mean well. The underlying theme? A woman’s value comes from how much she gives, how she looks, and whether she keeps the peace.
That’s a lot to carry. It’s not just the stress of juggling tasks or hitting deadlines. It’s feeling like no matter what you do, you’re never quite enough—never thin enough, kind enough, productive enough, or selfless enough.
This constant striving can wear you down, turning everyday stress into something chronic. And if it’s not addressed, that’s how burnout sets in.
There’s actually a name for this: “human giver syndrome.” In many cultures, women are expected to give endlessly, while men are more often allowed to just be—free to chase their own dreams and needs.
It’s not just unfair. It’s damaging. When women are always giving, there’s little left for themselves. Completing the stress cycle? Nearly impossible.
And it’s not just at home. Workplaces often add to the load, expecting women to handle emotional labor—like smoothing over conflicts, remembering birthdays, or organizing office events—on top of their regular jobs.
At home, even when both partners work full-time, the household and caregiving often still fall mostly on women.
Now, here’s something hopeful—these cultural scripts aren’t set in stone. Recognizing them is the first step toward change. When women realize these pressures aren’t personal flaws but society’s expectations, they can start to push back.
That might mean setting boundaries, asking for help, or simply admitting, “Hey, I have needs too—and that’s okay.”
No one should have to do this alone. Supportive relationships make a huge difference. Connecting with others who get what you’re going through—whether it’s friends, support groups, or online communities—can help you feel seen and understood.
Sharing your story can break through the isolation that often comes with burnout.
But let’s be honest—real change takes more than just individual effort. We need bigger cultural shifts, too. That means pushing for fair policies at work, challenging old stereotypes, and supporting groups that stand for equity and well-being.
Until then, self-compassion is your secret weapon. Treating yourself with kindness—especially when you feel like you’re falling short—can help silence those inner critics.
Remember, it’s not about ignoring your responsibilities. It’s about knowing your limits, and understanding that rest, joy, and self-care aren’t luxuries. They’re essentials for everyone.
